cards.title: Availability judgments · letter positions and causes of death
cards.aim: Do people judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind?
cards.manipulated: The letter question (r first versus r third) and paired causes of death (for example, botulism versus asthma).
cards.measured: Choosing which alternative is more frequent or more likely.
cards.found: About 70% say more words begin with r, though words with r third are three times more common. Many pick the dramatic cause of death over the more common one such as asthma.
cards.means: Ease of remembering is used as a cue for probability, and it is affected by things other than frequency.
cards.trap: Memorable or newsworthy is not the same as common.

cards.title: Representativeness · Robert, Jack, and Linda
cards.aim: Do people use resemblance instead of base rates and probability rules?
cards.manipulated: The description given (Robert, Jack, Linda) and whether base-rate information was available.
cards.measured: Judging occupation (librarian or farmer; engineer or lawyer) or choosing between bank teller and feminist bank teller.
cards.found: Many call Robert a librarian despite about 2.2 million farms versus 120,000 libraries. People use the 70/30 base rate alone but ignore it once Jack is described. About 82% choose the conjunction for Linda.
cards.means: A fitting description can override base rates and the conjunction rule.
cards.trap: Feminist bank teller is a subset of bank teller, so it cannot be more probable.

cards.title: Hospital samples · extreme proportions and sample size
cards.aim: Do people consider sample size when judging how often extreme proportions occur?
cards.manipulated: Hospital size: about 45 births per day versus about 15 births per day.
cards.measured: Choosing which hospital has more days with over 60% boys (larger, smaller, or about the same).
cards.found: 56% chose about the same. The correct answer is the smaller hospital, because small samples vary more.
cards.means: Small samples are more variable, which is why the law of large numbers matters.
cards.trap: The question is about days over 60%, not total boys born.

cards.title: Lord and colleagues · myside bias in article evaluation
cards.aim: Does an existing opinion change how the same evidence is evaluated?
cards.manipulated: Participants' opinion on capital punishment: in favor versus opposed.
cards.measured: How each participant interpreted the same article.
cards.found: Each side saw the article as favorable to its own position.
cards.means: Myside bias is evaluating evidence in a way that favors one's own opinions and attitudes.
cards.trap: Both groups read the same article. The difference is in the readers.

cards.title: Hidden number rule · confirmation and diagnostic tests
cards.aim: Do people look for evidence that could prove their hypothesis wrong?
cards.manipulated: Nothing varied between groups. Participants wrote their own number triples starting from 2, 4, 6.
cards.measured: Their triples and the rule they proposed, with feedback on whether each fit the experimenter's rule.
cards.found: The most common hypothesis was increasing intervals of two. The actual rule was three numbers in increasing order.
cards.means: Testing only triples that fit the hypothesis keeps a too-narrow belief alive. Testing for contradictions is more useful.
cards.trap: Repeated 'yes' feedback does not separate the narrow rule from the broader one.

cards.title: Jellybeans · favorable counts versus winning probability
cards.aim: Do people choose by the number of winning items or by the probability of winning?
cards.manipulated: Two bowls: 1 red bean out of 10 versus 7 red beans out of 100.
cards.measured: Which bowl participants chose before drawing.
cards.found: Most chose the 7-out-of-100 bowl, though 10% beats 7%.
cards.means: A larger count of favorable items draws attention away from the total number of draws.

cards.title: Ritov and Baron · convoy rerouting and lives saved
cards.aim: Do people choose the option that saves the most lives when it requires causing harm?
cards.manipulated: Rerouting a food convoy (saves 1,000 at the second camp, 100 die at the first) versus keeping the route.
cards.found: 63% did not choose to reroute. Some would keep the route even if only one person would die after the change.
cards.means: Reluctance to cause harm can outweigh a larger benefit, so choices are not just about the biggest number.
cards.trap: Net lives saved (900) favors rerouting, yet most refused.

cards.title: Tetlock and colleagues · taboo and tragic outcomes
cards.researcher: Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, and Lerner (2000)
cards.aim: How do taboo and tragic tradeoffs affect moral outrage?
cards.manipulated: Tradeoff type (taboo: Johnny's life versus hospital money; tragic: two children, one liver) and outcome (Johnny saved or not saved).
cards.found: In the taboo tradeoff, not saving Johnny produced much greater outrage than saving him. In the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar whether he was saved or not.
cards.means: The effect of the decision depends on the type of value conflict (an interaction).
cards.trap: A tragic tradeoff compares two sacred values. A taboo tradeoff puts a sacred value against a secular benefit.

cards.title: Ginges and colleagues · payment, recognition, and sacred commitments
cards.aim: How do people react to compromise deals over contested issues, and does money help?
cards.manipulated: Deal type: taboo, Taboo+ (one billion dollars a year for ten years), and symbolic (recognition and an apology). Participants were also classified as moral absolutists or not.
cards.measured: Anger, disgust, and support for violence.
cards.found: For moral absolutists, adding money increased anger, disgust, and support for violence. Non-absolutists responded the other way. Symbolic recognition lowered anger or disgust and violence support.
cards.means: Money can backfire when the issue is sacred, and symbolic reciprocity can help.
cards.trap: Samples were 601 settlers, 535 refugees, and 719 students.

cards.title: Iranian online study · sacred values, funds, sanctions, and energy results
cards.researcher: Dehghani, Atran, and colleagues (2010); Dehghani, Iliev, and colleagues (2009)
cards.aim: Do incentives or sanctions make Iranians who hold a sacred value more willing to give up the nuclear program?
cards.manipulated: A 2 x 3 design: program type (energy or weapons) by deal type (Taboo, Taboo+ with 40 billion dollars, Taboo- with the threat of sanctions).
cards.measured: Personal approval, anticipated public anger if the government approved, and whether the deal seems misleading.
cards.found: For sacred-value participants in the energy condition, approval was lower with funds or sanctions than with the basic deal, and anger was highest with funds. Participants without a sacred value rated approval higher and anger lower.
cards.means: For a sacred commitment, improving the material balance does not make a deal more acceptable.
cards.trap: Sacred means refusing the exchange no matter how great the consequences. About 14% (energy) and 13% (weapons) did so.

existing_explainers.title: Base rates and Jack
existing_explainers.plain: Start with how common each category is, then adjust for the description, instead of ignoring the numbers.
steps: Write the base rate (70 lawyers, 30 engineers).
With no description, the chance of an engineer is 30 out of 100.
With a description, remember the group still has more lawyers.
Do not decide on fit alone.
existing_explainers.example: Jack is conservative, careful, and enjoys home carpentry and math puzzles. People say engineer, yet the group is 70 lawyers.
existing_explainers.watchOut: A good-fitting description does not settle the probability.
explain: A base rate is how common each category is in the population. When you judge what category someone belongs to, the starting point should be those numbers, and a description should adjust them, not replace them. This is hard because a description is vivid and a base rate is a dry number, so the description tends to push the number out of the judgment completely.

In a group of 100 people with 70 lawyers and 30 engineers, one person picked at random has a 30% chance of being an engineer, and people get this right. People use base rate information if it is all that is available, but when a description is available they disregard the base rate.

Jack is a 45-year-old man, married with four children, generally conservative, careful and ambitious, and uninterested in political and social issues. He spends most of his free time on hobbies, including home carpentry, sailing and mathematical puzzles. People say Jack is an engineer, because his careful nature and love of puzzles fit the engineer stereotype, and that fit outweighs the base rate. But nothing in the description rules out a lawyer. A lawyer could be careful and conservative and enjoy puzzles, and the group still contains many more lawyers than engineers. The 70 and 30 are still true after reading about Jack, so the description has to be weighed against them and cannot settle the question by itself.

A party of 100 people, 90 in the chess club and 10 on the basketball team, makes the point clear. One person picked at random is tall, quick on their feet and loves jumping, and almost everyone guesses basketball because the description sounds like a basketball player. But 90 chess club members fill the room, and with that many people, plenty of them are tall, quick and love jumping too. Before any description, the chance of basketball was 10 out of 100. The description pushes the guess up from that low starting point, perhaps by a lot, but it has to be very convincing to end up above even. A good fit makes basketball more likely than it was a minute ago, not more likely than chess club. The crowd's numbers say where to begin and the description says how far to move.

This is the representativeness heuristic, judging class membership by resemblance. Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and people say librarian and ignore that America has about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries. Farmers far outnumber male librarians, so even if Robert's traits are somewhat more common among librarians, a randomly picked man is much more likely to be a farmer. The mistake in every case is letting the vivid description replace the dull numbers entirely.

existing_explainers.title: Conjunction rule (Linda)
existing_explainers.plain: Adding a condition can only shrink the set, so a combination is never more likely than one part.
steps: Name the two events (bank teller, feminist bank teller).
See that feminist bank tellers are inside bank tellers.
The smaller set cannot be more probable.
existing_explainers.example: About 82% chose feminist bank teller, but bank teller alone must be at least as probable.
existing_explainers.watchOut: A more detailed story feels more likely but is not.
explain: The conjunction rule says that the probability of two events occurring together cannot be higher than the probability of either single event alone. A conjunction means two things being true at once. The rule is easy to state and easy to break, because a more detailed story feels more likely even though it is less likely. Each added detail narrows the possibilities, and narrower things are less probable.

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright, and she majored in philosophy. As a student she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and she also took part in antinuclear demonstrations. People are asked which is more probable: that Linda is a bank teller, or that Linda is a bank teller who is active in the feminist movement. Because Linda sounds like a feminist, the second option feels more like her, and 82% pick it, which breaks the rule.

The groups show why. Everyone who is a bank teller makes up one large group, and some of those people are active in the feminist movement while many are not. The feminist bank tellers are a smaller group sitting inside the larger group of all bank tellers. Anyone in the smaller group also belongs to the larger one, so the larger group can never have fewer members, and a group contained inside another can never be more probable than the one containing it. Bank teller alone must be at least as probable as feminist bank teller.

Nested regions on a map work the same way. A friend who is in a coffee shop in Chicago is in Illinois, so the statement that she is in a Chicago coffee shop is true only when the statement that she is in Illinois is true. Illinois is a large area, Chicago sits inside it, and the coffee shop sits inside Chicago. Each added detail draws a smaller region that holds fewer of the places she might be, and she could be in Illinois in a hundred ways that have nothing to do with Chicago. A detailed story can feel more believable because it paints a clearer picture, but it can only be equally likely or less likely than the broader version it lives inside.

The error is the representativeness heuristic. Linda resembles a feminist, so the resembling option is judged more likely and people stop thinking about the sizes of the categories. How well a story fits a person says nothing about whether a combination can be more probable than one of its parts.

existing_explainers.title: Sample size (hospital question)
existing_explainers.plain: Small samples swing more, so extreme proportions happen more often in them.
steps: Note the sample sizes (about 15 versus 45 births a day).
Note the true rate is about 50% boys in both.
Ask which sample can stray more from 50%.
Pick the smaller one.
existing_explainers.example: The smaller hospital has more days over 60% boys. 56% wrongly said about the same.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Do not confuse total boys with the share of days above 60%.
explain: Sample size controls how far a percentage can drift from the true rate by chance. A town has two hospitals. In the larger one about 45 babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about 15. About 50% of all babies are boys, but the exact percentage varies from day to day. For one year, each hospital recorded the days on which more than 60% of the babies born were boys, and the question is which hospital recorded more such days: the larger, the smaller, or about the same.

Most people get this wrong. Fifty-six percent said about the same, and the larger and the smaller hospital were each chosen by 22%. The reasoning is that both hospitals have the same true rate of about 50% boys, so both should have unusual days equally often. That fixes on the 50% that applies to both and overlooks that the question is about day-to-day variation, which depends on how many babies are born each day as well as on the average rate.

With about 15 births in a day, chance can easily tilt a day heavily toward boys, so a day with more than 60% boys happens fairly often. With about 45 births, chance variations even out over more births, and the share of boys stays nearer 50%. The smaller hospital therefore records many more days over 60% boys, and the correct answer is the smaller hospital.

A basketball player who makes about half her shots over a season shows the same thing. In a game with only six shots, one or two lucky bounces put her well above half, and that happens in plenty of games. In a game with sixty shots, lucky and unlucky shots keep canceling each other out, and finishing above 60% would take unusual luck for a long stretch, which is rare. Her ability is the same in both games. What differs is how many chances there are for luck to even out. The six-shot game is the small hospital, the sixty-shot game is the large one, and the days above 60% are the unusually lucky games.

The law of large numbers states that the larger the number of individuals randomly drawn from a population, the more representative the resulting group will be of the entire population. A small random sample can be thrown off by a few unusual cases, so it may differ a lot from the population. The true rate describes the long run and does not promise that every short stretch will look like it. People who answered about the same expected every sample to look like the population, which is the representativeness heuristic applied where sample size matters.

existing_explainers.title: Probability as a ratio (jellybeans)
existing_explainers.plain: Chance of winning is winning items divided by total items, not the count of winning items.
steps: Write each bowl as red out of total.
Convert to a percentage.
Compare the percentages.
existing_explainers.example: 1 out of 10 is 10%. 7 out of 100 is 7%. So the first bowl is better, although most picked the second.
existing_explainers.watchOut: A bigger count of red beans hides the larger total.
explain: Your chance of winning is the number of winning items divided by the total number of items, not the number of winning items. The error comes from the fact that a count is easy to see and a proportion takes a little work, so people judge by what looks like more.

In the jellybean study, participants could earn up to $7 by receiving $1 every time they drew a red jellybean, and each time they chose between two bowls. One bowl held 1 red jellybean out of 10, so the odds were 1 in 10. The other held 7 red jellybeans out of 100, so the odds were 7 in 100, or 0.7 in 10. One in 10 is 10% and 7 in 100 is 7%, so the first bowl gives the better chance of a red bean. Yet most participants chose the 7 in 100 bowl. It has more red beans, seven instead of one, so it seems to offer more chances, even though it also holds many more white beans that hide those reds.

Their choice was influenced by considerations other than probabilities. People paid attention to the number of winning beans instead of their proportion, and by choosing by appearance they lowered their real chance of winning.

Two raffles at a school fair show the same trap. In the first drum there are 20 tickets and 3 win, and in the second there are 100 tickets and 12 win. Twelve winning tickets sounds far better than three, but a ticket is one single pull from the drum, and what matters is how crowded the drum is with losers. Three winners out of 20 is 15 out of every 100, which is 15%, and 12 winners out of 100 is 12%. The small drum with fewer winners is the better bet, because its winners make up a bigger share of what you might pull out.

A count of winners means something only once you know how big the whole pile is. Writing each option as winners out of total, converting to a percentage, and comparing the percentages avoids the error, and the red counts alone should never be compared.

existing_explainers.title: Expected utility
existing_explainers.plain: Weigh how good each outcome is by how likely it is, then choose the best total.
steps: List the alternatives.
Rate the value of each outcome.
Combine value with chance.
Choose the maximum expected utility.
existing_explainers.example: Casino gambling shows people choosing an activity despite knowing the odds are against them.
existing_explainers.watchOut: People value things other than money, so the theory does not fully describe choices.
explain: Decision making means making judgments that involve choices between different courses of action. Utility is the measure of how good an outcome is for the person who chooses it, referring to outcomes that are desirable because they are in the person's best interest. An option with higher utility leads to a better outcome for that person. Expected utility theory begins from the claim that people are rational. It holds that if people have all the relevant information, they will make the decision that results in the maximum expected utility, where expected utility combines how good each outcome is with how likely it is. In its early form, utility meant maximum monetary payoff, so the best choice was the one that paid the most money on average.

The procedure is to multiply the value of every possible outcome of an option by its probability, add the products, and pick the option with the largest total. The advantage is that the approach offers specific procedures for determining the best choice and tells what a fully rational decision maker would pick. That makes it a benchmark against which real choices can be compared.

Deciding each morning whether to carry an umbrella, with a 30% chance of rain, works this way. Carrying it costs a small, certain annoyance. Leaving it at home costs nothing if the sky stays dry, but a soaking and a ruined afternoon if it rains. The question is not only whether it will rain but how much each result would matter and how likely it is. If getting soaked bothers you a great deal, even a 30% chance of it can outweigh the small nuisance, so you carry the umbrella. If you will be indoors all day, the soaking matters little and you leave it. No money is involved. The values are how good or bad each outcome is to you, and the chances act as weights on those values.

The comparison with real behavior shows the limits of the theory. Utility is not necessarily money, because people find value in other things, such as safety, fairness or how they feel about a choice. People are not utility maximization machines. They gamble in casinos all the time even though they know the odds are very much against them, because they value the thrill or the chance at a big win. How a choice is worded can also pull them away from the larger total.

The refugee convoy dilemma makes the point sharply. Sending the convoy to the second camp would save 1,000 people but cost 100 in the first camp, so rerouting has utility 1000 minus 100, which is 900, and not rerouting has utility 100 minus 1000, which is minus 900. Expected utility theory says to reroute. Ritov and Baron (1999) found that 63% did not choose to send the convoy to the second camp, because actively causing harm weighs more than failing to prevent a larger one. The theory is a strong standard but a weak description of how people really choose.

existing_explainers.title: Inductive evidence strength
existing_explainers.plain: Inductive conclusions are probably true, and they are stronger with better observations.
steps: Check how representative the observations are.
Check how many there are.
Check how good (compelling) each one is.
Allow that one strong case can contradict a claim.
existing_explainers.watchOut: More observations is not the only factor. Quality counts.
explain: Inductive reasoning is reasoning based on observations, going from particular cases to a general conclusion. Scientists do this deliberately, making observations, collecting data and proposing a general rule that fits the many cases they have seen. Ordinary people do it constantly too, predicting what will happen from what has happened in the past, and some of it happens automatically, without deliberate thought. The conclusion is only probably true, never definitely true, so the real question is always how strong the support is.

Three things decide the strength of an inductive argument. The first is the representativeness of the observations, meaning how well they stand for the whole category. Many observations from a narrow group can still lead to a wrong conclusion, so a big pile of evidence from one corner of a category does not help much. The second is the number of observations, since more observations give stronger support. The third is the quality of the observations, since careful and accurate observations count for more, and sometimes one very compelling, high-quality observation can carry a lot of weight.

Reviews of a new pizza place show all three. The conclusion being built is that all their pizzas are great, a general claim drawn from the few pizzas other people happened to try. If every review comes from people who ordered the same cheese pizza on Friday nights, a hundred of them still say little about the rest of the menu, because they do not stand for the whole category. Twenty reviews support the conclusion better than two. One detailed review from someone who tried many dishes and described them carefully can count for more than a pile of one-line ratings.

Quality can outweigh quantity because an inductive conclusion is a general claim built from particular cases. One clear counterexample, such as one soggy, burnt pizza from that kitchen, can prove it false however many happy reviews came before. That is why inductive conclusions are always open to revision, and why a new observation can overturn a conclusion drawn from earlier ones. Judging an inductive argument means checking how representative the observations are, how many there are, and how good each one is.

qa_facts.q: How do decisions, judgments and reasoning relate, and what is inductive reasoning?
qa_facts.a: A decision is the process of choosing between alternatives, and reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions. Decisions are based on the judgments people make, and inductive reasoning is one of the primary mechanisms involved in making judgments. Inductive reasoning means reasoning from observations to conclusions that are probably, but not definitely, true. It is the basis of scientific investigation, where observations are made, data are collected and conclusions are drawn. The strength of an inductive argument depends on the representativeness, number and quality of the observations. Many white swans support an expectation about swan color, but one clearly observed black swan contradicts the claim that every swan is white, so a single high-quality observation can carry substantial weight. In everyday life, people use past experience to predict what will happen, especially in familiar situations, and some of this induction happens automatically.

qa_facts.q: What is a heuristic, and how do the availability and representativeness heuristics differ?
qa_facts.a: Heuristics are rapid rules of thumb that use past experience to guide present behavior. They are likely to give a correct answer but are not foolproof, because they reduce the amount of information a person considers by relying on a readily available cue, which usually fits the situation but can point away from the correct judgment. The availability heuristic judges by how readily examples come to mind, and the representativeness heuristic judges by how much a case resembles a category. The difference is which property supplies the shortcut, accessibility in memory or similarity to a familiar kind of case.

The availability heuristic makes events that are more easily remembered seem more probable. The more examples a person can think of, the more probable the event seems. That is useful when memorable events are frequent, but memorability is also affected by distinctiveness, emotional salience and frequent encoding or retrieval, none of which make an event more common.

qa_facts.q: How do the r-words and causes-of-death judgments show the availability heuristic?
qa_facts.a: In the word judgment, about 70 percent of respondents say English has more words beginning with r than words with r as the third letter, but words with r third are actually three times more common. Retrieving words by first letter is easier, so those words feel more numerous. For causes of death, asthma is more likely than botulism or a tornado, yet many pick the less likely cause. A death from botulism can become front-page news while deaths from asthma go virtually unnoticed, so distinctive coverage makes the unusual cause easier to bring to mind.

qa_facts.q: What is the representativeness heuristic and base-rate neglect, and how do the Robert and lawyer–engineer problems show it?
qa_facts.a: The representativeness heuristic bases a judgment on how much one event resembles another, so a person decides whether A belongs to class B from how well A’s properties match what is normally associated with B. Base-rate neglect is when that similarity displaces the background prevalence of the categories. Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and many people say he is more likely a librarian than a farmer. But America has about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries, so the base rate favors farmer. In the lawyer–engineer problem a group has 70 lawyers and 30 engineers. With no other information, the chance of an engineer is 30 out of 100 and people use that correctly. When Jack is described as conservative, careful, ambitious and enjoying home carpentry, sailing and mathematical puzzles, people tend to call him an engineer. So base rates are used when they are all that is available and disregarded once descriptive information is given.

qa_facts.q: What is the conjunction rule, and why is the Linda problem an error?
qa_facts.a: The conjunction rule states that the probability of two events occurring together cannot be greater than the probability of either event alone, since every case satisfying both conditions also satisfies each one. Linda is described as single, outspoken, bright, trained in philosophy, concerned with discrimination and social justice, and involved in antinuclear demonstrations. About 82 percent choose Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement over Linda is a bank teller. The extra detail makes the description fit the person they were told about, but feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers, so being in the smaller set automatically puts her in the larger one. The error is picking the better-fitting story over the nested-set probability relationship, which is a representativeness effect.

qa_facts.q: In the hospital problem which hospital has more days with over 60 percent boys, and what does the law of large numbers say?
qa_facts.a: The larger hospital has about 45 births a day and the smaller about 15, and about half of babies are boys. The question is which hospital records more days when over 60 percent are boys, and the correct answer is the smaller hospital. The most common response was about the same, chosen by 56 percent, which ignores how many births are behind each day’s percentage. Smaller samples vary more, so an extreme proportion is more likely in the group of 15 births, while the larger hospital’s daily proportion is more stable. Choosing the larger hospital confuses the absolute number of boys with how often an extreme proportion occurs. The law of large numbers says that as more individuals are randomly drawn, the group becomes more representative of the population. People often expect small samples to be representative too, which understates how much a small sample can vary.

qa_facts.q: What is an illusory correlation, and how does it connect to stereotypes and availability?
qa_facts.a: An illusory correlation is a relationship that appears to exist even though it does not exist or is much weaker than assumed. Stereotypes are oversimplified generalizations about a group, often emphasizing negative characteristics, and they direct attention to behaviors that fit the expected description. Selective attention and remembering the matching instances make the stereotype feel supported, so the apparent evidence is shaped by what was noticed and retained. The link to availability is that stereotype-consistent behaviors are easier to bring to mind because they got particular attention, and their availability is then mistaken for evidence that the behavior is strongly associated with the group.

qa_facts.q: What is myside bias and confirmation bias? What did Lord and colleagues (1979) find, and how does the 2, 4, 6 task show confirmation bias?
qa_facts.a: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek information that fits a hypothesis and overlook information that argues against it, and myside bias is one form of it, generating and evaluating evidence and testing hypotheses in ways biased toward one’s own opinions and attitudes. Lord and colleagues (1979) had people who favored capital punishment and people who opposed it read the same article. Those in favor interpreted it as favorable to their position and those against interpreted it as favorable to theirs, focusing on agreeing information and disregarding the rest. In the 2, 4, 6 task, participants get 2, 4, 6 as an example of a hidden rule, write their own sets of three numbers, get feedback only on whether each fits the rule, and then propose the rule. The most common hypothesis is increasing intervals of two, and testing only sequences that fit it gives repeated yes feedback. But the actual rule is any three numbers in increasing order, so only trying to disconfirm, testing the boundaries, would reveal the narrow belief is wrong.

qa_facts.q: What is expected utility theory, and why does it not fully describe what people choose?
qa_facts.a: Utility refers to how desirable an outcome is because it serves the person’s interests. Expected utility theory assumes people are rational and, with all relevant information, choose the alternative with maximum expected utility, combining the value of possible outcomes with their chances, and the monetary version uses the maximum expected monetary payoff. It gives specific procedures for determining the best choice. But people find value in things other than money, and many decisions do not maximize the probability of the best outcome, so people are not utility-maximization machines. Casino gambling is an example, because people choose it despite knowing the odds are strongly against them.

qa_facts.q: What happens in the jellybean problem, and what does it show?
qa_facts.a: Participants earn one dollar whenever they draw a red jellybean, up to seven dollars, and choose between two bowls. One bowl has 1 red bean out of 10, a 10 percent chance, and the other has 7 red beans out of 100, a 7 percent chance. Most participants choose the 7-out-of-100 bowl. The larger number of red beans is attractive even though the probability of drawing one is worse. A larger number of favorable items draws attention away from the denominator, the total number of possible draws, so the decision depends on considerations other than the actual probabilities of winning.

qa_facts.q: What happened to travel after September 11, and what does it show about risk decisions?
qa_facts.a: After September 11, air travel decreased and driving increased. The probability of dying in a car accident is much greater than while flying, and the reported number of Americans who died on the road while avoiding flying exceeded the total number of passengers killed on the four hijacked flights. Avoiding the feared event increased exposure to a more likely danger, because the emotional impact of the attacks is a different basis for a decision than the relative probabilities.

qa_facts.q: What is the convoy dilemma, and what did Ritov and Baron (1999) find?
qa_facts.a: A convoy of food trucks is traveling to a refugee camp during a famine, and rerouting saves 1,000 people at a second camp but 100 people in the first camp die. Rerouting has the better net count, 1,000 − 100 = 900 versus 100 − 1,000 = −900. Ritov and Baron (1999) found that 63 percent did not choose to reroute, and some would keep the original route even if only one person at the first camp would die. Reluctance to cause a loss can outweigh the larger number saved elsewhere.

qa_facts.q: What is the Sacred Value Protection Model (Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green and Lerner, 2000), and what are taboo and tragic tradeoffs?
qa_facts.a: The Sacred Value Protection Model of Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green and Lerner (2000) proposes that people want to protect what they hold sacred, and that sacred values are compartmentalized separately from secular values. A taboo tradeoff intermingles the sacred and secular domains, so treating a sacred concern as exchangeable for a secular benefit feels threatening and provokes moral outrage. A tragic tradeoff compares two sacred values with each other, and people are less morally outraged by it. In the taboo scenario, Robert can save Johnny, a five-year-old needing a liver transplant that costs the hospital one million dollars, or spend the money on equipment and salaries to recruit talented doctors. In the tragic scenario, two children need a liver but only one is available.

qa_facts.q: What did Tetlock and colleagues (2000) find about moral outrage in the Johnny scenarios?
qa_facts.a: In Tetlock and colleagues (2000), moral outrage was rated for taboo and tragic tradeoffs, with separate outcomes for saving Johnny and not saving him. Under the taboo tradeoff, not saving Johnny produced much greater outrage than saving him, and choosing other uses for the money instead of the child’s life received the strongest negative response. Under the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar whether Johnny was saved or not, because choosing either child leaves another sacred concern unmet. So there is an interaction between the type of value conflict and the decision made within it.

qa_facts.q: What did Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) study, and how did money and symbolic offers affect moral absolutists and non-absolutists?
qa_facts.a: Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) studied sacred-value tradeoffs in an ongoing political conflict, with 601 Israeli settlers, 535 Palestinian refugees and 719 Palestinian students. They offered three deals. The taboo deal asked Palestinians to recognize the sacred and historic right of the Jewish people to Israel, with two states and a Palestinian state in 99 percent of the West Bank and Gaza. Taboo+ added a material incentive, one billion dollars a year for ten years paid by Israel. The symbolic version added Israeli recognition of the historic and legitimate right of Palestinians to their own state and an apology for wrongs done. Moral absolutists treat the issue as a sacred value and reject compromise regardless of benefit, about 46 percent of settlers for never giving up part of the Land of Israel and about 54 percent of the students for the right of return and Jerusalem. Non-absolutists also have strong preferences against compromise but do not treat the issues as sacred. For absolutists, adding money increased anger, disgust and support for violence, while for non-absolutists it reduced them. Symbolic recognition was associated with lower anger or disgust and lower support for violence, so material benefit and symbolic reciprocity are different.

qa_facts.q: What did Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010) study, and how were sacred values measured?
qa_facts.a: Dehghani, Atran and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev and colleagues (2009) studied sacred values in relation to Iran’s nuclear program, asking whether people who hold the program sacred would accept material benefits or costs in exchange for compromise. An incentive offers a benefit for agreement, and a sanction is a disincentive that imposes a cost for refusing. The online study had 1,997 Iranian participants, in Farsi, and measured approval, anger, and whether a proposal seemed misleading. Using a measure based on Baron and Spranca (1997), the sacred-value response is that giving up the program should not be done no matter how great the consequences, and about 14 percent for nuclear energy and 13 percent for nuclear weapons chose it.

qa_facts.q: What were the deals in the study by Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010), and what happened for participants with a sacred value?
qa_facts.a: In the study by Dehghani, Atran and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev and colleagues (2009), the design was 2 × 3, energy or weapons crossed with three deals. Taboo had Iran give up the program and its facilities to the United Nations in return for Israel doing the same, Taboo+ added 40 billion dollars from the United Nations to Iran, and Taboo− added the threat of additional sanctions if Iran refused. Participants rated their own approval, whether people would be angry if the government approved, and whether the deal seemed misleading. For energy, participants with a sacred value showed lower approval with the financial incentive and with sanctions than with the baseline, and anticipated anger was highest with the incentive and elevated with sanctions. Participants without a sacred value had much higher approval and lower anger, with little variation across conditions. So for a sacred commitment, improving the material balance does not necessarily improve acceptability.
